One user found the output style easier to read: "I don't know about token savings, but I find the 'caveman style' much easier to read and understand than typical LLM-slop."

Reaction to the Claude skill: unsure how much it will cut costs, but "it will make my day not to have to read through entire essays about some trivial solution. tldr; Claude skill, short output, ++good."

A developer worried about token costs on their own project (an infra bundle generator) said the skill gave them a laugh and some useful ideas. They called the claimed 75% reduction "insane" and starred the repo.

Critique of the skill's design: its trigger description is ironically verbose. The phrase matching could be a UserSubmitPrompt hook using regex and additionalContext, and /caveman already invokes the skill directly anyway.

Critic argues that for LLMs, tokens are units of thinking. Forcing the model to be concise limits the computation available to it, so "by demanding the model to be concise, you're literally making it dumber." They note that separate thinking modes partly mitigate this.

Skeptic says you'll rarely blow your token budget on output. Input is the real bottleneck (skills, directory trees, code files, tool outputs), while output is usually a few hundred lines of code plus a short explanation.

User tried talking caveman-style to Claude themselves. They felt the answers got worse, with more misunderstandings, sometimes needing more total words to re-explain instructions, and typos doing more damage with less context.
Security concern about the repo: "What is that binary file caveman.skill that I cannot read easily, and is it going to hack my computer."

Commenter says the author ignores the system prompt and the extra inference work the skill adds. In their view it's only worth using if you like the response style, since real optimizations happen in model training and infrastructure.

Benchmark author ran 24 prompts across 5 arms with rubric-based judging. Prepending "be brief." matched Caveman on tokens (419 vs 401-449) and quality (0.985 vs 0.970-0.976). They credit Caveman with consistent output structure, intensity modes and the Auto-Clarity safety escape, but say compression itself isn't the differentiator.

Negative take: "Caveman is useless for me... speaks like an idiot. I don't want to interact with an idiot. It's irritating." This user prefers plain "Be brief": "easy, no setup needed, not another mindless mumbojumbo extension."

Critic says saving a couple hundred output tokens is negligible in coding sessions that use hundreds of thousands of tokens. The skill's own tokens also have to be counted. Funny at release, but treating it as a useful optimization is "cargo culting."

Commenter argues that talking through a problem in depth is integral to how Claude Code reaches results. Those aren't "wasted tokens," so Caveman only sounds clever if you don't understand LLM reasoning.
Light positive: "Caveman made me laugh and that, in theory, should count for something."
